utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Josse, I do understand that you would like to raise two issues, one very brief procedural one, another one taking a bit more time and necessarily raised in private session. Would you agree if we do that after the first break?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. In fact. . That would suit Mr. Harmon, who needs to be present for at least one of those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's do it after the first break. But I had forgotten to ask the registrar to call the case. Mr. Registrar, would you --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. So therefore at this moment we could continue the examination-in-chief of Mr. Kapetina. Mr. Kapetina, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Josse, would you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, the first thing I want to ask you about this morning -- or this afternoon, more to the point, relates to international law and your role in advising the army to respect, for an example, the Geneva Convention. What personally did you do in that regard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that after the National Assembly session on the 12th of May in Banja Luka was held, we started drafting the regulations and provisions with regard to respect for international war law. And within the frameworks of that activity the ministry prepared three provisions, the first of which was an order on the application of the provisions on the international war law with the president of the republic of the head of the country, and also two further instructions and guidelines by the president of the republic about conduct on prisoners of war and instructions with respect to the application of the Geneva Conventions. And I took part, of course, in the elaboration of these provisions. All the provisions were passed by the end of June that same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to help at all as to how, if at all, these provisions were disseminated among the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those provisions were urgently distributed right up to the level of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and the duty everybody had was that the commander -- or rather, the commander of the Main Staff had the obligation of issuing orders that those provisions reach every man down the chain of command to the lower formations and units. This set of instructions - they weren't long instructions, they covered just one or two pages - that they should reach each and every member of the Army of Republika Srpska, and that's what was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, may I seek, in order to better understand the testimony of the witness, some clarification. You used the words "international war law" several times in one of your answers, and you referred to the Geneva Conventions and the applicability of the Geneva Conventions. Is it your testimony that because the armed conflict ongoing was of an international character that the Geneva Conventions would apply, or would they apply for any other reasons, apart from the character of the armed conflict? Could you be a bit more specific in that respect before we continue with how these decisions and how these regulations were conveyed to the troops.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not pass those provisions because the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina had the character of an international conflict; it was in fact a war conflict and the rules, and regulations of international war law provide for conduct within a war and the conflicts in war. So that's why we incorporated that law into the conflict that we had. It wasn't of an international character, but nonetheless the international war law does provide for and prescribe for conduct in conflicts generally. So we decided to apply those provisions to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm afraid it has not fully clarified my question, because again you are talking about international war law, which seems to be a reference to the law applicable in international war. Or would you say the international law applicable in domestic or in armed conflicts of a non-international character? Because there, of course, the international law -- at least the Geneva Conventions would not fully apply.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said that we otherwise in our army, in the Yugoslav People's Army, that is, respected the special rules governing conduct in a war conflict. We had special manuals with these rules written down, and from the conventions I mentioned we took over the sections dealing with conduct towards prisoners of war and civilians and the rights of civilians during a war and the rights of civilian protection during a war. So we incorporated all that, took them into account, and drafted our own provisions and instructions for the army's behaviour and conduct, which means that we didn't take over the entire code of the international war law, but just what could be applicable to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We took that over and incorporated them into the three provisions that I spoke about earlier on. Perhaps there was something additional, but I can't think of that at the moment. They weren't any broad provisions; they were very succinct ones and fitted in the space of two pages, the instructions and provisions, so that they could be used as a pocket edition, if I could put it that way, which every soldier could carry in his pocket. And the basic premises of war law and how soldiers behave towards civilians, towards prisoners of war, towards the members of the civilian protection, civil defence system, and so on and so forth, towards international organisations or representatives thereof. And I think I've clarified that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether it has been fully clarified is another matter, but I'll -- I'll refrain from asking further opinion. You have not been called as an expert on legal matters, and apart from that there's an old Latin saying "ius curia novia," which means the Court knows the law. Judge Hanoteau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe you've already said this earlier yesterday but I forgot, who took the initiative to write down this regulation and who took the initiative of circulating it? Maybe you're going to repeat what you said already, but I don't remember what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I mentioned it. I don't know where the basic idea came from, who it came from, but I do know that the task was set by the minister of defence, who was Bogdan Subotic. So most probably it was his idea or whether it was perhaps suggested to him by somebody else, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but could you tell us exactly. You said that you weren't many in the ministry, maybe two only, two people. So how were you asked to do it? Were you called? Did you get a written instruction to do it? Or did you just talk with the minister, you know? Could you please elaborate on this, if you remember, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said was that the minister said that we should urgently undertake the preparation of these provisions. Of course we had very scant literature on the subject at Pale. However, as I say, from the previous systems, that is to say, the system on -- in the Yugoslav People's Army, those rules and regulations did exist. Provisions about international war law, the Geneva Conventions, and so on. So with the scant literature that we had at our disposal at that time, we undertook to prepare those three provisions with the material we had at hand. I think that at that time we had a number of people in the ministry, five to ten people, who were engaged in the implementation of the provisions, but they worked in Sarajevo in the ministry there, like I did myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there was no need for the Assembly to intervene; it was just circular letters that were sent, regulations, and it was under the mandate of the ministry, right, it was their competence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. It was the Ministry of Defence that had the duty of preparing the regulations. The first order was signed, as I said, by the president of the republic, Mr. Karadzic, and then we distributed all those regulations up to the level of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. And the commander of the Main Staff further issued orders for the distribution to call units lower down, and to each and every rank-and-file soldier. I think those regulations exist. I don't think they've been lost. And you can see all the provisions and regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps you should make this clear, Mr. Kapetina. You've already told the Chamber that you are a political scientist by training. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I graduated from the faculty of political science in the department for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've had no formal legal training. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any formal training, but I was included in the drafting of provisions, both at federal and republican level, mostly provisions within the field of planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's also clear from your evidence that you have spent the whole of your professional life working as a civil servant in the field of defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. For almost 20 years I worked in the state administration, and all my work -- years of work I devoted to matters of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, you have given some evidence a few moments ago about the drafting of various documents and directives in relation to international law. I now want to ask you about what information came to your knowledge, and indeed the knowledge of the ministry, in 1992 about crimes being committed by soldiers in the field?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that whole year of 1992, you had different periods and different situations in which the state administration of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had to work, and the Bosnian Herzegovinian government and Serbian republic thereof. For example, the period of May, when I came to Pale, and perhaps until the end of July or perhaps even the end of August, the territory on which the government -- in which the government worked and its departments of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was to all intents and purposes cut off from the other parts which were under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. I, of course, am not in a position to demonstrate this to you on the map, but I'll try and do my best to explain it to you. The government from Pale controlled practically the entire area up to the Sokolac municipality and Vlasenica as well. The Serbian municipality in Sarajevo could not be controlled because they were cut off. The roads had been cut off, and there was a by-road that was being built. But Podrinje and all this area was cut off, and you had to -- could only reach those municipalities via Serbia and Montenegro. Now, as to the municipalities in the Banja Luka region, Banja Luka, Prijedor, Doboj, that general area, you could only communicate with that area when the corridor was broken through at Brcko. So that was the period, May, June, July 1992. And I spoke about the communication road network. I said that all the other communications were down as well, all the other means of communication, so that the government during that period of time did not have a complete insight into the situation on the ground, nor did any reports come in on any regular basis about the situation in the areas under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska so that the government didn't know, in fact, about many of the events and crimes that had been committed. It was just not informed about those things. When I say "the government," of course I mean that in addition to the government and its departments at Pale, there was also the Presidency that was located at Pale and the president of the National Assembly. So as I say, that was the objective situation that reigned during those three or four months; of course later on the situation improved. But throughout the year of 1992 that was how it was. For example, the government didn't have any links in connection with Herzegovina at all during that time. There was no road communication; you couldn't reach the area by road. You couldn't get to the municipalities in the Herzegovina region. As I say, the situation improved later on by the end of 1992 and especially in 1993 when there was a greater compactness in the area under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you've given a long - the Chamber will think - useful background to communication problems. How did that impact on knowledge of what was going on in the field? Perhaps I should be a bit more specific. So far as crimes are concerned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I forgot to mention in my answer to your question the fact that the army was actually being created in the second half of June and in the month of July. It was under creation, so that the army wasn't fully organised yet either. It didn't have all the formations and units that the law provided for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, I'm going to stop you. You spent a very, very long answer by giving all kind of circumstances which might have prevented information to reach Pale. The question was whether any information reached. You made a distinction between what roads were closed, what routes to go, et cetera. You told us that in June -- May, June, July the situation was different; and then you said later on that it remained the same during the rest of the year. The question is quite simple: What information was received about crimes committed? And perhaps, since you made the distinction, what information was received in May, June, July? Any information, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to speak in concrete terms. Throughout 1992, from May when I started working in the ministry until the end of 1992, not a single piece of information reached the ministry about war crimes committed in the field, not one single piece of information. We had certain instructions, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not asking about instructions. I was, at this moment, seeking to find out whether any information reached you. You said: "It did not reach the ministry." Are you aware of any such information reaching the government, apart from specifically the ministry you worked in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I know is that there was a problem with the government as well because the government had no information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether there was a problem for the government. I wanted -- I asked you whether your answer specifying that the Ministry of Defence in May, June, July did not receive any information; whether, as far as you know, the same is true for the government as a whole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, this related to the whole government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we go to the remainder of the year. We are now in August up till December. Was any concrete information received by your ministry, to start with, about crimes committed in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Ministry of Defence to the end of 1992 didn't receive a single piece of information coming into it from the field about any crimes having been committed nor about any prisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, same question as far as the whole of the government is concerned. August and following months, 1992. Any information received on crimes committed or, as you said, prisons? And if I could extend that to camps as well. Any information for the whole of the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, when the Ministry of Justice was formed of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and when a man was put in charge of penitentiaries and supervising penitentiaries, he did submit a report to the government. And that's when that question started to be debated at government meetings. So this assistant in the Ministry of Justice compiled a report, which I didn't read, I'm afraid, on the situation in penitentiaries and correctional centres. And then the government was informed about such things for the first time, about the situation in those facilities, in prisons, the existence of prisons, and so on. But I didn't have that information to hand. And I don't know which period this applied to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would this information not reach the ministry in which you worked, apart from you personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I interrupt, Your Honour. Does Your Honour mean and did this information or should it have done -- would this information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's not clear in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I should be more specific. Are you aware of this information you just talked about, which was then, as you said, subject of debate, did that reach your ministry as well, apart from whether it reached you personally at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the information was prepared and a report was prepared for a government meeting and was on its agenda, then my minister would have had an information of that kind because he attended government meetings. I, myself, could not ask to be given that material, material from government meetings, and as the minister offered to give them to me myself. So I didn't have an insight about it and I didn't read the report, but I did hear that it was up before a government meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So where you earlier said that the Ministry of Defence to the end of 1992 didn't receive a single piece of information coming into it from the field about any crimes having been committed nor about any prisons, then that would not necessarily include information that came through this report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Josse. Judge Hanoteau has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I don't understand in your testimony is the following: The ministry you were working for, what connection was there between the -- your ministry and the army? You said there was no information provided on the crimes that were committed or on the prisons that existed. However, was there any regular contact between your ministry and the army in those areas where it was difficult to communicate? In other words, let me be more specific. Does this mean that the military was totally cut off from the field and cut off from their men in the field, or was nonetheless one way of communicating or another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Ministry of Defence was not in the chain of command of the military, so the minister of defence did not make any decisions relating to command in the army. The ministry did have a relationship with the army as far as logistics was concerned, and also there was some relations in the army that were under the authority of the Ministry of Defence. I don't think that the commander of the Main Staff informed the defence ministry about everything. Some things they probably informed the president of the republic directly. So we did not receive all the reports from the Main Staff commander; the minister of defence did not receive them. We had reports from his assistants regarding logistics requirements in the army, also perhaps some things relating to promotions, appointment to certain posts, and so on and so forth. So we were not cut off from the army. We did communicate on these matters, but we were not authorised to command. That was in the jurisdiction of the president of the republic, but we did have duties in regard to the logistics matters and supplying the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means you did not communicate over any such matters as combat operations or military assignments that were -- or military operations that were unfolding at that time. In other words, the Ministry of Defence did not receive any such reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. We did not receive any reports about operations, about battles. And under the law, the army was not obliged to give us these reports. There was no General Staff section within the Ministry of Defence; that section was in the Main Staff. And that section was directly responsible to the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I apologise, but I'd like to ask a question related to this to the witness. Witness, you extensively explained to us that no reports about what happened in the field as far as crimes are concerned were received, and you explained extensively that that was because of communications and transportation problems. You also told us that the instructions as how to behave in the conduct of warfare were disseminated up to the lowest levels. What I do not fully understand yet is that communication seems to be working, at least -- and if you give these instructions that it reach -- that it reaches the lower levels, whereas the communication in the other direction would be totally blocked, as -- from what I understand. Could you explain -- so apart from whether you had any authority in -- in the operational sense why instructions could be communicated to the lowest levels and why there was no way of receiving any information, whatever that information would have been, from the lower levels up again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will try to explain. Instructions that I spoke about, which you mentioned, were sent only up to the Main Staff, and the Main Staff was at Han Pijesak and the communications went to Han Pijesak. So those regulations or those instructions, we would copy them, multiply them, and then send them to the Main Staff. And then the Main Staff was supposed to distribute that using its own lines down to the corps, and then the corps was going to pass that on to the lower-ranking units and so on and so forth. The Main Staff was obliged to send it to seven points, which is where the corps were. And then the corps was supposed to pass them on to lower-ranking units. This wasn't a perfect system. There were problems there, but the army had helicopters, other means; the state did not. I know that all the communications that we had with Herzegovina were carried out by choppers via Montenegro and not through Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's how these communications proceeded. I would like to explain something else, too. In peace nobody commits a crime publicly; crimes are always concealed. That's why we didn't have any information about these crimes. Nobody publicly committed any crime and then announced that through the media. Crimes were generally committed covertly. Nobody publicised that. If we knew about such problems, we would -- had we known that, we would have informed the military prosecutor's office and the military courts, and then we would have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In your explanation you now give a totally different reason for not receiving that information, because, as you say, it was concealed. Earlier you said that the instructions were signed by Mr. Karadzic, and then we distributed all those regulations up to the level of the Main Staff of the army. And the commander of the Main Staff further issued orders for the distribution to call units lower down, every rank and soldier. When I asked why messages would not go up through the same communication channels, I now understand your testimony to be - but please correct me if I'm wrong - that it was not that there were no communication channels, but people would -- that those who may have been committed crimes would have concealed those crimes, and that for that reason it did not go up in the same communication channels. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that we didn't have information about crimes until the end of 1992. I assume why this information was not reaching us. It's an assumption. We practically did not have a single piece of information or any insight about what was going on in the field regarding crimes or any camps; that is the truth. I assume why information, specifically about crimes, were not reaching the ministry or the organs of power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's be clear that assumptions should be known as such, because you came up with the assumption first that communication channels and road transportation would have prevented these -- this information to reach the other levels, whereas now we have a totally different assumption, and that is that the -- those who were committing those crimes would have concealed them. I'm not saying that either of them is true or not true, but let's not forget that these now are assumptions and should not be confused with facts. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about one specific area in this regard, and this might be outside of 1992. Do you have any knowledge of Mr. Subotic visiting Bratunac at any time during the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't have the information that Minister Subotic visited the Bratunac municipality, so I really cannot talk about the time frame either. I don't have that information. I don't know that he visited the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, did he ever discuss with you the fact that he had been there and been shown at least one Muslim grave?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minister Subotic never told me about his visit to Bratunac or any details relating to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about him visiting Muslim graves in general? Can you help about that at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I asked you yesterday about an expanded Presidency, and you told us what you knew of the Presidency of the republic through 1992. I want to ask you how, as far as you understand it, Mr. Djeric fitted in to the scenario, and in particular the expanded Presidency, if at all.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Djeric was the prime minister. He wasn't a member of any expanded Presidency, neither the regular Presidency or the expanded Presidency. He was simply the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you be given the bundle, please, and turn to tab 8. This is the decision on establishment of the supreme command of the RS army. It's dated the 30th [realtime transcript read in error: "13th"] of November of 1992 and signed by Dr. Karadzic. It's being exhibited in this case as P64A. Firstly, Mr. Kapetina, what was the supreme command as you understood it? What -- by that I mean the supreme command set up by this document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The supreme command established with this document was an advisory body of the president of the republic or presidents of the Presidency at the time. So it advised the president of the Presidency relating to command matters and the army. So the command is exclusively an advisory body of the president or the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What makes you say that it was purely an advisory body?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that because it was not authorised to make any command decisions. According to the law, it was an advisory organ of the presidents of the Presidency. After the supreme command there was a supreme council that was established that also had an advisory function.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This political command structure was set up for what reason?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was established for the purposes of consultations and advice to the Presidency and the president of the Presidency so that we would be able to make decisions relating to army command. Although I never attended a supreme command session, but I did attend sessions of the Supreme Defence Council and mostly some topical issues were discussed. The question of command was discussed least of all. Matters that were discussed were some civilian matters, relations between the civilian and the military parts, and so on. Any decisions that were in the sphere of command were never discussed at the sessions which I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear there. You were talking about the sessions of the Supreme Defence Council that you attended. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I did not attend sessions of the supreme command, but I think in 1993 it was when the Supreme Defence Council was formed. And whenever I attended these sessions, I know that questions relating to military command were never discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm a little bit lost, Mr. Josse. I would need some further explanation. This Supreme Defence Council was established in what year and who were the people or the members of this defence council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly when, but during the war, during the conflict, instead of the supreme command, the Supreme Defence Council was established. It was more or less of the same composition as the supreme command. Occasionally I attended those Supreme Defence Council meetings, and I said that at the meetings there was never any discussion about command of the military. The supreme command was practically not functioning. This was a very brief period. Later the president of the republic took over the command of the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not totally convinced by this answer. Mr. Josse gave us -- submitted a document which is dated 12th of November, 1992. Is that correct? Tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 13th of November, Your Honour. The transcript's just said "13th," I said "30th," 3-0.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this body is called "the supreme command of the RS army." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [In English] Of the RS army -- [Interpretation] There was another body and a similar body which was established. I think that's what you were saying, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of the conflict the supreme command grew into the Supreme Defence Council; this is what I wanted to say. And the Supreme Defence Council had the same function as the supreme command. In item 5 of this decision, it says what the role of the supreme command is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did it include the same members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Supreme Defence Council and the supreme command, completely identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Up till the 30th of November of 1992 when the supreme command was established, who had jurisdiction over operational matters within the armed forces of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The supreme commander of the military until the adoption of this decision and on the adoption of this decision was the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And to clarify that. When you say "on the decision," you mean after the decision the position was the same. Is that right or have I misunderstood you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Until the adoption of this decision and after the decision was adopted, the supreme commander was the president of the republic, one person. And of course this applied throughout the whole conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to comment on the power and influence the president of the republic had over operational matters in the field?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in the president's cabinet, so I assume that he did receive reports from the Main Staff commander. And then based on those reports, he was probably able to and had an overview of the situation in the field, the situation in the army, what was going on at the front, and so on. These reports were not sent to the defence minister, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What power did the Assembly of the republic have over its armed forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The republican Assembly didn't have any power over the military, the Army of Republika Srpska. The only thing it did was to adopt the law on the army and the defence. It did not have any direct competencies over the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the president of that Assembly? What power did he have over the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Assembly also did not have any competencies or power in relation to the Army of Republika Srpska. He was simply a part of the Assembly, and he presided over the Assembly. The Assembly and the president of the Assembly had the same competencies. So as president of the Assembly, he didn't have any authority over the Army of Republika Srpska. The function of the Assembly was purely legislative.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Specifically I want to ask you about what involvement, if any, Mr. Krajisnik had in the passing of the law on defence that you were, for the most part, responsible for writing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly -- or the deputies had no influence over the law during its drafting stages. The draft laws were submitted by the government. The government was proposing them. The Assembly simply adopted them. I wasn't at the Assembly sessions to know what the debate was like. I know that there were amendments to this law, but in the drafting stage I know that the Assembly had no input at all on these two bills.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, my question relates specifically to Mr. Krajisnik. Is the position the same for him as the answer you've just given?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course the president of the Assembly and also the deputies. None of the deputies took part in the drafting stages of this law. The Assembly receives a draft for its consideration, and they can also submit or propose amendments to this draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A number of specific questions about Mr. Krajisnik. Did you have any personal dealings with him prior to your arrival in Pale in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any person dealings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: After your arrival in Pale, did you have any dealings with him, again personally, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I had no personal or official dealings with Mr. Krajisnik. My first contact with him was - I don't know exactly what period this was - was when the Assembly concluded that it was necessary to adopt an urgent law on military courts and military prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I don't know the time period, but I know that I was invited to President Krajisnik's office and that I was told that there were these conclusions, that we needed to quickly adopt laws on the military courts and military prosecutor's office, that this was a matter that had to be brought urgently before the Assembly. There were already some questions about competencies in relation to military personnel and soldiers. So this needed to be done as soon as possible. What the competencies were of military courts and prosecutor's offices and what were the competencies of civilian-such organs, this had to be done together with the justice ministry. The draft proposals for these two laws had to be done very urgently.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about dealings that Mr. Krajisnik had with the Ministry of Defence in general in Pale in 1992, rather than with you specifically? Can you help us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know of any dealings or specific relations between the president of the National Assembly with the ministry. I think that he did not have any dealings or special relations vis-a-vis the defence ministry. I even know that Minister Subotic told me that he had some relationships and was being invited by President Krajisnik. And if we -- actually, if we received invitations, they were from the president of the republic to deal with the situation in the army. And I and Mr. Subotic never said they were invited by Mr. Krajisnik, the president of the National Assembly, whether they were called by him to discuss any problems. So that was -- he -- they were not called --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I had nothing to do with dealings with the ministry of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, similar to the correction, you just quoted to saying: "I even know that Minister Subotic told me that he had some relationships and was being invited by Mr. Krajisnik." Is that what you just said, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, you are quoted in English as having just said, and I quote: "I even know that Minister Subotic told me that he had some relationships and was being invited by President Krajisnik." Did you just say that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that. I said that Minister Subotic never told me that he was called by President Krajisnik. And I said that the ministry had no relationships and dealings with the president of the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's what I had -- that's how I have been so advised, that's why -- obviously why I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's perfectly clear, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In short, in 1992 what power did Momcilo Krajisnik have over the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No authorisations, no power.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you briefly, if I may, about what happened at the time of the Dayton Accords and the departure of the Serbs from Sarajevo. Were you involved in a commission at that time dealing with this issue?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On behalf of the Ministry of Defence I was a member of the board for the implementation of the Dayton Accords for the Sarajevo region.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you liaised, among others, with Mr. Krajisnik in that regard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I don't know what function. Possibly President Krajisnik was in that board or -- well, he was either a member of it or a -- the president of it. I don't know what his post was. I, myself, was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What stance did you personally take on the Serbs' departure from Sarajevo? Specifically, did you try and persuade Serbs to leave?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean my personal attitude?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm, first of all, asking you about your personal attitude.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know what the attitude of the board was, what stance it took. I could have any separate stance with regard to the board.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Fine. What stance did the board take, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The board's stance was that all avenues be explored and see if the people couldn't be kept in the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what, as far as you are aware, was Mr. Krajisnik's stance on this issue?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely the same as the board, to exhaust all possibilities and to keep the Serb people in Sarajevo or, rather, in the municipalities in the area of Sarajevo and Serb Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take your time, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That concludes my examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope it won't be seen as too lawyer-like if my answer is yes and no. And to give you a full response, I would ask to address the Court briefly in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kapetina, Mr. Tieger would like to address the Court in your absence. It must be some kind of a procedural matter, I take it. May I invite you to follow the usher but to remain standing by until we have heard what Mr. Tieger tells us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I raise again the issue of the 65 ter summaries. Let me say this in brief. With respect to those matters brought to our attention through the 65 ter summary or through subsequent e-mails, indeed, no matter how terse or non-detailed, I'm prepared to proceed and intend to do. With respect to the issue raised in this session, in particular about communications and knowledge of crimes, to the best of my recollection and re-confirmed to the extent that I could by a review of the 65 ter summary and any subsequent e-mails, that matter was not brought to our attention. For that reason, I want to reserve the right to review, at least overnight, the testimony and prepare for any appropriate cross-examination on those subjects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's perhaps first establish, does the information about crimes committed in the field is included anywhere, in your view, in the 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, I'm going to concede that. My only observation is that I do contend -- it's slightly bizarre that the Prosecution are not in a position to cross-examine a witness about an issue as central as that in a case such as this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse tempts me to say it's slightly bizarre to hear a witness like this come in and deny any knowledge of crimes. It takes a considerable amount of effort to amass the materials that are available to cross-examine properly on that subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I would have asked you, Mr. Tieger, whether you were ready to start cross-examining the witness, the answer would have been yes, I take it. Let's be very practical at this. Let's start the cross-examination. Let's see how far it brings us, and let's see whether nature resolves the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I assist in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- one regard. This probably isn't assistance at all to anyone. But the next witness will not be in this building today. In other words, I won't be in a position to call him until tomorrow. He will be available to begin his evidence tomorrow afternoon but not today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That makes it even more serious in terms of waste of time, Mr. Josse. Because if Mr. Tieger would finish his cross-examination on all the other subjects, we would be forced to wait until tomorrow before we could continue, if the Chamber would grant the request by Mr. Tieger. But at the same time, Mr. Tieger is invited to consider how solid the information was on whether or not information was received either by the Ministry of Defence or by the government, as a whole. I mean the following: That if you would confront the witness with information that has reached, well, let's say the government or whatever document, the witness said, as far as he knows -- and one could not expect a witness to know everything that happens in the Ministry of Defence, although it was small, neither to know everything that happened in the government. But please think it over. Let's get started with the cross-examination for the first ten minutes, and let's then see whether your request still stands, whether the matter is resolved already by time, and the Chamber will then give a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just ask. Would Your Honour like arrangements to be made for the next witness to be brought to this building?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say anything without knowing what Mr. -- how much time Mr. Tieger thinks he would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I say, Your Honour, I would much rather call him tomorrow, but I'm determined, we're determined, not to lose any more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Our time is extremely precious, and if need be, I will get him here. Or arrange for him to be brought here, I think is a better way of putting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we will need some time for the procedural issues after the first break. How much time do you think you would need for the cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult to say, Your Honour, but certainly a session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's a session, that would fit -- if I would look at what's not a rule, but the 60 per cent guidance, that would bring you to approximately two hours, that's a little bit over one session. Then noting that we would have another -- we'll have another -- let me just see. We'll have two -- another two and a half hours. You might need some time for the procedural issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We will need to fully explore one of the procedural issues before the next witness begins, commences his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That becomes a certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's little chance -- I take it that there's a fair chance that you would approximately finish this witness, even having heard the procedural issues, by today. Let's proceed for this moment. And, Mr. Josse, the Chamber does not require you to take any additional measures at this moment for the next witness to arrive in this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very helpful, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so the Court is aware, I'll try to make an assessment at the end of the next session or at any relevant point during that about how much progress I'm making in light of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- issues intended to cover as well as an ongoing assessment of the need for additional time related to the issue I discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the parties are invited both to intervene when a witness seems to dwell on a lot of subjects, apart from the subjects that is the core of the question. I did it a couple of times, Mr. Josse. I think that there have been moments where you might have considered to do it yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll try harder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, thank you for your patience. Mr. Tieger, counsel for the Prosecution, will start his cross-examination. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kapetina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yesterday you described in response to questions by Mr. Josse the problems that you say you encountered at the Ministry of Defence in 1991, and specifically with the minister of defence. And you indicated in your testimony that as a result you decided to go public with that -- with those problems and those issues. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I wrote a written warning for the Presidency and cautioned the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the government of Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm not asking you, I apologise if I was misunderstood to recount your testimony again, simply to confirm with a yes or no whether that summary was correct. I would note for the record that at page 27 of the transcript yesterday you indicated that you decided to go public with that information, as I understood it, in the fashion you just began to describe. Is that essentially right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said it was my aim to inform the public about it all, but that the public did attend my warning. Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event, you indicated to the Court yesterday that you did so because of your concern as a professional, that you did so independent of others without being told to do so or pressure to do so by others. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in fact, it seemed that you wanted to stress that professionalism and independence as a way of assuring the Tribunal about the accuracy of your assessment of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time. Is that also accurate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask you to repeat that comment of yours, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll move on in the interests of time. We really are getting very close to the break. Mr. Kapetina, isn't the real fact of the matter that it was not your idea to send the letter, but it was the idea of the SDS and SDS officials?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The real truth of the matter is that it was my initiative and my letter. I just held consultations with the vice-premier Dr. Simovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Isn't it also a fact, Mr. Kapetina, that you were effectively activated by the party in 1991 and thereafter followed party instructions and engaged in performing tasks for the party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true that I was activated by the party in 1991 and that I performed any tasks for the party. And pursuant to instructions from the party in 1991, I was not a member of the party, that is to say, of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, membership of the party, Mr. Kapetina, and activities in pursuit of party objectives can be two different things, as we shall be discussing after the break. And finally, Mr. Kapetina, isn't it also a fact that you have not been fully accurate in describing to the Court the circumstances surrounding the mobilisation and recruitment issues that prompted -- that were the subject of your letter in 1991 or the circumstances that prompted the decisions by the Bosnian government in connection with mobilisation and recruitment in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I did explain that to the Trial Chamber yesterday. I didn't enter into the substance of the warning, and I didn't deal with questions of mobilisation and recruitment -- I didn't only deal with questions of mobilisation and recruitment in the warning, and I didn't explain that to the Court yesterday. I didn't even wish to comment the comments made in the journal Narodne Novine either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll talk about that shortly, but let me just before the break recall your testimony yesterday. You testified at length about your discussions with Minister Doko, or at least the discussions you say you had with Minister Doko in 1991. You testified at length about your alleged submission of inspection plans and his rejection or refusal to act on those plans. And then you said, again at page 27 of the transcript, that you decided to go public with this information by sending a letter and so on. Correct? I see you nodding, so I assume that that's a fair summary.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me warn you again. Maybe I said that yesterday, although I don't remember saying it, I didn't want to go public. I wanted state -- to caution state institutions about the implementation of the law. Now, the fact that this gained publicity is another thing. I personally didn't provide it to the media, to any of the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's not quibble in that case about the term "going public." We'll let the record speak for itself, along with your explanation now. Irrespective of that, what I've just recounted is essentially how you related the background to your letter. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this, you see: The situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time in the field of defence was far worse than I depicted it in my letter. It was much worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the substance of your letter. I just want to ask you whether or not it's correct that in describing the circumstances that gave rise to your letter, that is what you explained to the Court, that it was fundamentally your discussions with Minister Doko that triggered your determination to send a warning letter to the organs of government you described, that they were acting illegally.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. And my conversation with Mr. Doko and the overall situation in the field of totally national defence motivated me to write this letter to the Presidency and government because they were the most responsible organs for defence matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when we return after the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- we will explore our submission that that's a fundamentally misleading characterisation of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Mr. Tieger, before we have a break, would it not be fair to -- if you confront the witness with the reasons he gave to write the letter, that he gave two reasons, the one being the unlawful and unconstitutional behaviour of -- of his minister, who said that he would not respect the laws; and at the same time he also told us that he -- the witness feared that he might end up having problems if he did not inform the highest republican organs that there was no inspection in the republic, which is not exactly the same as that his personal problems that would result from that. Would it be fair to put that to the witness as the two reasons he gave?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honour, and I think the witness heard what the Court said and is certainly in a position to confirm or reject that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are the two reasons you gave, yes, because that's more complete than what you've confronted him with. We'll have a break, and we'll restart at a quarter past 4.00, but not for you. Mr. Kapetina, we, again, need some time for procedural issues. So the break presumably will take at least 10 to 15 minutes, if not even a bit more for you. We stand adjourned until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, if we would start with the one-minute issue, that could be done in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes please. I've had a chance to talk to Mr. Stewart about the general procedural remarks in terms of where the Defence case is going that Your Honour made yesterday. He's anxious for an opportunity to respond in person. He would invite the Court to set aside a short period of time at the beginning of proceedings on Friday, if that meets with the approval of the Court. That is my request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter and we'll let you know, or would you need an answer right away?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't need an answer right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then you'll hear from us -- unless there's you'd like to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Say if there is another time that is more convenient to the Chamber, then of course Mr. Stewart will make himself available, but he is anxious to address the Court orally on the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider it. If we would choose for another time, we will not do so without consulting Mr. Stewart first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could I mention one other matter in open session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- to some extent that has arisen during the break and it relates to scheduling in one sense. The witness after next, not Mr. Kapetina, not the witness thereafter, but the witness after that who is not seeking protection, and I am not going to mention him by name for reasons that will be clear in a moment. He is in The Hague. We were aware that he had bouts of ill health. That had made his attendance a little bit uncertain. He's arrived here, mentions health problems to us. A member of our team was speaking to him at some length today, broke that meeting off so that the witness could have a break, which was thought necessary. The victims and witness service have contacted -- well, me personally during the break to say that he is no longer fit for further proofing today. They have said that he is sufficiently unwell, if I can put it like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That may have some affect on the schedule. He'll undoubtedly need more breaks than normal when he gives his evidence; I had already been advised of that. That's all I can say. I don't suppose it's very helpful, but at least I'm forewarning the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, it goes without saying that -- and even with full respect for the privacy of the witness, of course the Chamber is more inclined to be very flexible if it knows a bit about the background, about the source, if there's any objective support for what is presented as a -- not feeling well. I'm not saying that we could not accept that, but of course it's better for us to assess to what extent we should take that into consideration if we have more information about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We will work on that. The reason I mention it is because the information is coming in one sense from an objective source, namely the witness assistant who has been looking after him for the last couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although perhaps not medically trained, but being a human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if there's -- I take it that if there's any need for medical assistance, that the Victims and Witnesses Unit will provide that or at least to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In my limited experience, Your Honour can rest assured about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's good to have that re-affirmed in court. Then we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger, once the witness has entered the courtroom and has taken his seat, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, as I feared, it took a little bit longer. Again, thank you for your patience. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetina, let's begin by taking a look at the intercepted telephone conversation that you listened to yesterday, the one involving Dr. Karadzic and yourself on July 1st, 1991. That's found at tab 4 of the Defence binder. Mr. Kapetina, before I direct your attention to any particular portion of that conversation, let me ask you: That was not the -- yesterday was not the first time you had a chance to see the transcript of this conversation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it wasn't the first time. I saw it when I had the interview with the investigators of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at that time, before they -- the investigators showed you the intercept, they asked you about contact you had with the SDS leadership in connection with the issue of the letter you sent, and you indicated to them, did you not, that you had not had contact with the SDS leadership in 1991 in connection with the letter you ultimately sent about the illegal -- allegedly illegal action of the Bosnian government?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said. I said I didn't have any contacts with the leadership of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turn to the intercept itself now, and if I can direct your attention to page 3 of the transcript. And I believe that's both in the -- in the B/C/S version and the English. After a discussion, introductory discussion, between you and Dr. Karadzic, you were explaining a little bit about the implementation of the ministry's function and so on. Dr. Karadzic says: "So I'm asking you to write an official record, that is, a report right now in your capacity as in inspector to the prime minister, to write a report, et cetera, et cetera." You point out that you can only address the government, that your competence only covers the government. And he says: "Look, please write this and send copies to the corps commander and the commander of the TO." And you say: "Well, I thought we should ask for an urgent meeting with the minister this morning and then he could put forward the concept and we would be informed of what he's doing." And Dr. Karadzic says: "You know very well what he's doing and the whole ministry knows -- or every ministry knows what he is doing." Mr. Kapetina, wasn't it the case that it was Dr. Karadzic who raised and insisted on the issuance by you of a formal protest or letter or record and that your idea at the time was just simply to call for a meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct that the initiative was for me to write the warning -- that the initiative came from Mr. Karadzic. That's not correct. If you will allow me to say this. I proposed -- well, I didn't put the proposal to Mr. Karadzic, but I proposed that a meeting be held of the staff of the ministry, because -- so that all of us could present our views to the defence minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Dr. Karadzic goes on in the course of that intercept, and if you look now at the bottom of page -- toward the bottom of page 3, he addresses your concerns about the extent of your competence and says to act instead according to your conscience urgently regardless of how far your competence reaches and tells you that you have the right to send a copy of your report to the government, et cetera, to the president of the council for national defence, the corps commander, the commander of the TO, as we see on page 4. And you say: "All right." And then he continues by saying: "Otherwise you'll be responsible," insisting that you carry out your function. And you say: "Agreed." That was the substance of that conversation, was it not, Mr. Kapetina, at least as it was recorded on July 1st, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Karadzic asks of me to write an official memo or report, which I didn't do. I didn't write an official note. I issued a written caution to the Presidency of the government on the fact that the constitution and law was not being adhered to, and that's quite different from an official note. An official note would have been to say that I wasn't doing my job and what the situation was like in the ministry. I did not write that. Secondly, I didn't accept the suggestion made by Mr. Karadzic that I send a copy to the commander of the Main Staff and the other people mentioned there, because I saw that Mr. Karadzic doesn't understand my position in the Ministry of Defence, and that is why I asked for a meeting with Simovic, who knew full well what my competence and authority was, what position I held and whom I could address.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And after talking with Mr. Simovic, you did send a letter to all the parties mentioned by -- at least you sent a letter that went to Mr. Izetbegovic and you copied it to all the parties mentioned by Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only sent a caution to the government and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, no one else. I didn't send it to anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you sure about that, Mr. Kapetina, or is it possible that you did send copies to the other parties? Because that's what you indicated in your interview. You weren't sure; it may have happened.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not -- I wasn't asked that question during the interview. The question I was asked, whether other sides had it. I don't know. I said yesterday that everybody was a member of the council for national defence, and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina received my letter along with an invitation to attend a meeting. And they received it from the secretary of the council, along with an invitation to attend the meeting with the meeting's agenda. And I categorically state that I did not send my letter of warning to anybody else but the institutions. I didn't send it to the media either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to dwell on this point, but I would note that at page 14 of the interview conducted on July 13th, 2004, you were asked specifically: "Did you send an identical report to the prime minister, the corps commander, and the TO commander?" And your answer was: "I don't think so. And if I did send them, if I did send something to them, then it was just an information because I didn't really cooperate with them. They were not under me." Is that a fair answer? Sorry, that's not a good question. Is that what you said and does that more accurately reflect your recollection of what was sent?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that's the way I put it, but you can see from that that I did not send anything to the institutions that you are insisting on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I take it that there's an audio-recording of this interview if -- if the parties would feel that it's of such importance to verify the words of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- during the interview. Mr. Kapetina, there is an audio-recording of that interview. So if you -- I don't know, the Chamber might not take any action proprio motu, but at least there is a possibility to verify this. And if you feel uncomfortable with the matter, or if one of the parties would feel uncomfortable with the matter being not verified, there's an opportunity to do so. I just inform you about this so that you know that there is a technical possibility. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At tab 2 of the Prosecution's exhibits, there's a conversation of a -- a conversation that took place between Mr. Simovic and Mr. Karadzic. It may not be necessary to direct your attention to particular portions of that, Mr. Kapetina. Mr. Simovic indicates in that conversation to Dr. Karadzic that a meeting was scheduled with the Council for All People's Defence because of certain initiatives regarding recruits, particularly the public warning by you, which he describes as "quite a good job." Does that conform with your own recollection that your written warning triggered a meeting of the Council for All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The meeting was not organised or scheduled because of my warning. My warning was just one item on the agenda. The meeting had a much broader significance and there was several items on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So in any event, your public warning was at least part of the agenda for that meeting and part of the impetus for that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was part of the agenda, but it was not the reason that the meeting was held. It could also have happened for it not to be on the agenda at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's move on, if we can, quickly to the circumstances that were extant at the time of these conversations, July and August of 1991. Now -- and before I address that, let me turn quickly back to your conversation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, number 2 of the exhibits has not been assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 2 would be P1036, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if I understood your testimony correctly yesterday, you indicated or testified that Minister Doko told you that he wanted to or hoped to effectively destroy the JNA in Bosnia by preventing or forestalling your inspections. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that Doko told me that the JNA would be destroyed if the inspections were not held. I said that there was a certain task and a plan. My personal feeling was that within that plan there was a way to do it, but not through inspections.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the issue of your inspections and whether or not they were conducted had no impact on this plan you're alluding to. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it did. I said what I found later out about Minister Doko's plan. I could have prevented that plan from being implemented, had I gone and toured about 20 different facilities, if I had 20 inspectors to take with me. In this way many other plans could be thwarted as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's be as clear on this as we can. You were not responsible for inspecting the combat-readiness or preparation of the JNA, were you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you were not responsible for inspecting the combat-readiness or preparation of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KAPETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, have you -- done with Exhibit 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at tab 2, which is P1036, Mr. Kapetina, Mr. Tieger confronted you with a portion of that telephone conversation, but I'd like to invite you to also comment to another portion of that conversation. I think it's third box from the bottom in B/C/S of page 1, and in English it is page 1, the seventh box from the bottom. Where when Mr. Simovic had informed Mr. Karadzic about the meeting of the Council for All People's Defence, Mr. Simovic says: "This inspector, Kapetina, I told him to do something," which, at least from the language, suggests that he instructed you to do something. Could you help us out whether you have any recollection of any instruction received from Mr. Simovic, and if so, what that instruction was about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggested to Simovic -- or actually, I informed him of what I was intending to do, and all I wanted from him was his opinion, whether he agreed with this, in the sense of: Would I have protection but not whether I would do that. However, the vice-president told me: Mr. Kapetina, whatever you do, you will be held responsible for it. There's nobody in this state who could protect you. The government cannot protect you, the ministers from the government cannot protect you. Whatever you do, you will be the one who will bear the responsibility for it. So I just informed them about what I wanted to do, and I was told: This is something that you're doing at your own initiative because you will not have the protection of the ministers, the Serbian ministers, in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So this portion of the intercept -- and in this portion of the intercept, Mr. Simovic does not adequately inform Mr. Karadzic on your conversation. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did not convey the conversation accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Sorry, Your Honour, just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
